title: Beyond the Machine: How Industrials Are Creating Customer Value with Digital and AI
gist: Industrial equipment makers, service providers and leasing companies have proven AI works internally and creates real customer value, but cannot get customers to pay for AI-enabled aftermarket offerings; BCG argues the binding constraint is commercial and organizational (pricing, technical sales, customer success, resourcing model), not technical, and prescribes a four-part go-to-market framework including capturing 25-30% of customer value created and land-and-expand SaaS motions.

insights.claim: Industrial companies (heavy equipment manufacturers, service providers, leasing firms) have largely completed the internal AI phase — field service, supply chain and pricing operations — and are now pivoting to selling AI-enabled products such as analytics subscriptions and AI-powered service packages to customers.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The externalization of industrial AI is the next revenue line to underwrite in capital-goods names; watch for disclosed software/subscription ARR rather than internal cost-savings claims.
insights.locator: Industrial companies, including heavy equipment manufacturers

insights.claim: For most industrial AI offerings, strong technical performance and demonstrated customer value have still not translated into direct monetization — end users adopt the tools willingly but resist paying for them.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Treat adoption/usage metrics disclosed by industrials as a weak proxy for revenue; ask specifically what share of AI users are paying users.
insights.quote: Customers acknowledge the value of AI-enabled aftermarket solutions and use them actively, but remain unwilling to pay for them.
insights.locator: As a result, companies often find themselves

insights.claim: The bottleneck to scaling industrial AI commercially is behavioral, commercial and organizational rather than technological — pilots frequently succeed while scaling across the sales force, operations and customer base fails.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Diligence should focus on the seller's commercial capability build (pricing, technical sales headcount, customer success) rather than model quality or data assets.
insights.quote: The barrier is rarely with the digital or AI solutions themselves; it is commercial, behavioral, and organizational.
insights.locator: Industrial companies are continuing to improve internal operations

themes.theme: Three customer objections that block payment

insights.claim: Industrial customers who already pay large sums for equipment assume AI, analytics and digital tools should be bundled in at no extra cost — a legacy expectation about what is 'included' that suppresses willingness to pay.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Attach-rate targets for software on hardware sales are structurally harder than SaaS comparables; discount management guidance that assumes easy bundled upsell.
insights.locator: Legacy expectations around what is

insights.claim: The most persistent objection to paying for industrial AI is data ownership: customers see raw machine data as inherently theirs and do not credit the vendor's investment in turning it into insights, predictions and recommendations.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Vendors whose pitch rests on owning the data flywheel are exposed; the defensible position is proprietary models plus embedded workflow, not the data itself.
insights.quote: Customers rightfully see raw machine data as inherently theirs, without fully appreciating the investment required to turn that data into actionable insights, predictions, and recommendations.
insights.locator: Confusion between data ownership and value creation

insights.claim: Compared with physical assets, software and analytics feel abstract to industrial buyers, so they hesitate to pay even when the value delivered is real.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect longer monetization ramps in industrial software than in native-SaaS end markets; model slower revenue recognition than management guides.
insights.locator: Skepticism about paying for intangibles

themes.theme: Value-based product design from day one

insights.claim: AI-enabled industrial offerings only command payment when they deliver specific prescriptive actions — identifying the problem asset, its cause and the fix — rather than generic analytics dashboards.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Screen industrial software products for prescriptive action output; dashboard-only products are unlikely to sustain subscription pricing.
insights.quote: This is the asset that is having a problem. Here’s what’s causing it, and here’s how to fix it.
insights.locator: Focus on driving business actions

insights.claim: Vendors should build customer-specific ROI models using tailored assumptions — plant size, operational baseline, and improvement potential — so value estimates feel concrete and credible rather than generic.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Presence of per-customer value-quantification tooling is a leading indicator that a vendor can convert pilots to paid contracts.
insights.locator: Quantify value impact

insights.claim: A global food processing machinery manufacturer overcame customer refusal to pay for its AI platform by embedding the AI into a redesigned production process with defined 'moments of truth', which shifted perceived value away from raw data toward workflow design and proprietary models — customers then opted into paid programs and became advocates for further features.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Process re-engineering, not better models, is the unlock for monetization; look for vendors that sell workflow transformation alongside the algorithm.
insights.locator: To shift this perception, the manufacturer redesigned

insights.claim: Leading industrials treat anchor customers as co-development partners — giving them prototypes populated with their own data and iterating on tiers and positioning — which produces both better products and higher willingness to pay.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Named design-partner programs in industrial software are a tangible early signal of future paid conversion.
insights.locator: Co-develop with customers to sharpen the offering

insights.claim: AI coding tools across the software development lifecycle now enable live product edits in real time with the customer present, which justifies lowering the quality bar for what gets shown to anchor customers in order to iterate faster.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Second-order effect of AI dev tooling: it compresses enterprise product-discovery cycles, advantaging vendors willing to demo work-in-progress.
insights.quote: AI tools across the software development lifecycle are making iteration faster than ever before, in some cases enabling live product edits in real time while working with the customer present.
insights.locator: Lower the bar for what is tested with anchor customers

insights.claim: Customers systematically overestimate their own operational performance, so peer benchmarking that exposes and then bridges the performance gap is one of the most powerful sales levers for AI-enabled solutions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Vendors with large installed bases can weaponize cross-fleet benchmarking data as a sales weapon — a scale advantage smaller entrants cannot replicate.
insights.quote: Customers often overestimate their own performance, believing they have no need for solutions that could improve it.
insights.locator: Help customers understand their starting point

insights.claim: A vehicle fleet leasing provider launched an AI platform for fuel efficiency, utilization and maintenance built around customers' own workflows through iterative co-development, and customers involved in the process became enthusiastic adopters for whom paying 'felt natural'.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Fleet leasing is an early-adopter vertical for monetized AI; watch leasing companies adding platform revenue on top of asset spreads.
insights.locator: A vehicle fleet leasing provider offers a useful illustration

themes.theme: Pricing architecture and value capture rate

insights.claim: BCG's benchmark is that providers of AI-enabled industrial solutions should expect to capture 25% to 30% of the value their solutions create for the customer, and customers will not pay that unless value is first proven through test labs, pilots and data-driven proof points.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete take-rate anchor for sizing industrial AI TAM: estimate customer value pools and apply a 25-30% capture ceiling.
insights.quote: A well-observed principle is that providers should expect to capture 25% to 30% of the value that its solutions create for customers.
insights.locator: Price services commensurate with value, and prove it

insights.claim: The standard industrial AI pricing model is a fixed subscription set at expected value that escalates on annual renewal as the customer accumulates evidence of impact, with explicit performance-based pricing as an alternative that is more attractive to customers but requires the vendor to directly measure realized value.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Built-in renewal escalators mean revenue quality improves with contract age — cohort ARR expansion is the metric to track, not initial deal size.
insights.locator: In practice, the standard model is a fixed subscription

insights.claim: Vendors must explicitly choose between a 'resourcing light' model (analytics and software with limited on-site support, lower price but more scalable) and a 'resourcing heavy' model (on-site customer success, deep integration, higher price and stronger renewal rates), because serving all customers identically under-serves some and over-invests in others.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The resourcing choice determines gross margin versus retention profile — a direct input to whether an industrial's software segment deserves SaaS-like multiples.
insights.locator: Choose your resourcing model and make it explicit

themes.theme: Sales motion, cycle length and organizational rebuild

insights.claim: The biggest observed pain point in monetizing industrial AI sits inside the vendor, not the customer: legacy sales organizations are unaccustomed to selling SaaS and lack packaging, pricing, customer-specific value quantification and marketing capabilities.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Even differentiated industrial AI offerings will miss revenue targets absent a rebuilt commercial org — a concrete short-side thesis on over-promising incumbents.
insights.quote: Companies that fail to build these internal capabilities will struggle to convert even the most differentialed offerings.
insights.locator: One of the biggest pain points we consistently observe

insights.claim: A dedicated technical-sales 'Quarterback' role — orchestrating account team, customer success and product teams through each moment of truth — is central to the industrial AI sales motion, alongside demos, customer-specific ROI models, value proofs and aligned internal incentives.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Hiring patterns for technical sales roles at industrials are an observable leading indicator of software revenue conversion.
insights.locator: Establish the technical sales motion

insights.claim: Industrials consistently underestimate the sales cycle for AI offerings because these are fundamentally enterprise software sales: customers need their own data in a working prototype, then a multi-site pilot, then setup support, and are gated by annual budget planning cycles that require proof points to exist before planning begins.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect guidance misses on industrial AI revenue timing; monetization lags pilot announcements by at least one customer budget cycle.
insights.locator: Plan for a longer sales cycle and customer budget cycles

insights.claim: Land-and-expand — securing a small paid foothold such as a structured pilot then growing coverage, functionality and price — is the winning motion, and while Salesforce and Adobe have mastered it, most industrials have not.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The commercial playbook gap between software leaders and industrials is the capability arbitrage; industrials that hire it in could re-rate.
insights.quote: Software leaders like Salesforce and Adobe have mastered this; most industrials have not.
insights.locator: Pursue a land-and-expand strategy

insights.claim: Free trials must be explicitly time-boxed with clear pricing and opt-out mechanics, because otherwise customers anchor on free and the offering never converts to paid.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Open-ended free access to industrial AI tools destroys future pricing power — a red flag in any 'users but no revenue' disclosure.
insights.quote: Free trials can support the “land” motion, but they must be explicitly positioned as temporary, with clear pricing, defined durations, and opt-out mechanics that prevent customers from anchoring on free.
insights.locator: Free trials can support the

insights.claim: Standard SEO is now insufficient for industrial vendors; they must deploy generative engine optimization (GEO), structuring content, FAQs and technical documentation so prospective customers' AI assistants surface their offering accurately.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: B2B demand generation is shifting from search rankings to AI-assistant retrieval — a structural headwind for SEO-dependent marketing spend and a new vendor category.
insights.quote: With the rise of AI, standard search engine optimization (SEO) is insufficient.
insights.locator: Deploy generative engine optimization (GEO)

themes.theme: Proof case: business model, not technology, was the blocker

insights.claim: An off-road equipment and technology provider saw adoption of a working pay-per-use AI solution stall purely because consumption-based pricing felt unfamiliar and risky to customers accustomed to owning equipment outright.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Business-model mismatch, not product quality, is the main adoption risk when shifting capital-goods customers to consumption pricing.
insights.locator: An off-road equipment and technology provider put this level

insights.claim: That off-road equipment provider fixed adoption by deliberately capping fees at no more than 25% of customer value created, running internal test sites for proof points, offering risk-free trials and retrofits, choosing a resourcing-heavy model with a dedicated customer success function, and training its dealer network on AI sales and support.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Dealer-network retraining is an underappreciated cost and moat in industrial AI distribution; capping value capture at 25% trades near-term price for adoption velocity.
insights.locator: The company responded with a systematic overhaul

insights.claim: The same off-road equipment provider is now piloting pay-per-outcome pricing where customers pay only if promised value is realized, explicitly to reduce adoption risk for skeptical buyers, and its adoption, customer satisfaction and revenue all accelerated after the commercial overhaul.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Outcome-based pricing is migrating into heavy industry; it shifts performance risk onto the vendor and requires measurement infrastructure — a new operational risk to underwrite.
insights.quote: the bottleneck was never the technology, but rather the sales process
